max_tire.note: Bronco Zone owners run 33x12.50R15 on 15x10 wheels on stock-height 1980–96 trucks. Some needed the bumper ends trimmed or shimmed, and there can be slight radius-arm rub depending on the wheel. 31x10.50 clears with no contact.
The bare minimum for 35s according to one Bronco Zone owner, who warns of a lot of tire-to-body contact off-road.
4 in of suspension lift is the better option for 35s, and 6 in is called optimal. Plan for TTB camber bushings and lower gears.
Needs serious fender trimming and strains the stock running gear.

items.title: Speed-control deactivation switch may overheat or burn
items.summary: The switch could leak internally and overheat. Dealers first disconnected the speed control, then reconnected it once replacement parts were available in 2006.

items.title: Speed-control deactivation switch (1993 trucks)
items.summary: The same overheating-switch problem on 1993 Broncos and F-Series, covered in two later campaigns.

items.title: Ignition switch internal short circuit
items.summary: The ignition switch could short internally; dealers replaced it.

items.title: Transfer case built with the wrong shift motor
items.summary: Electric-shift cases could slip out of 4-High when coasting or reversing; dealers replaced the transfer case.

items.title: Parking-brake self-adjuster pawl slips
items.summary: The pawl could skip teeth on the ratchet; dealers fitted a wedge to hold it in engagement.

items.title: Front bumper U-clip nuts can fracture
items.summary: The nuts that hold the front bumper to its inner arms could break.

items.title: Door latch release cable can freeze
items.summary: Water in the cable could freeze in sub-zero weather and make the door latch malfunction.

items.title: Spring-lock fuel-line coupling may not be engaged
items.summary: An incompletely engaged coupling could leak fuel.

items.title: Fuel-rail burrs may damage O-rings
items.summary: Burrs on the new EFI fuel rails could cut adjacent O-ring seals during assembly and cause fuel leaks.

items.title: Steering-arm knuckles improperly manufactured
items.summary: A knuckle could fracture and let the tie rod disengage.

items.title: Steel wheels may crack at the rim
items.summary: Some steel wheels were improperly manufactured and could crack without warning.

timeline.change: Second generation launches on the F-100 chassis: 104 in wheelbase, solid coil-sprung Dana 44 front, 9-inch rear, 351M standard and 400 optional, lift-off half hardtop. 77,917 built.
Rectangular headlights standard on all trucks; catalytic converters added; 104,038 built, the best year of the full-size run.
Third generation on the new F-150: Dana 44 Twin Traction Beam front, 300 six standard (manual only), 302 returns, 400 dropped. 1980–81 frames are lightened with stamped holes.
Stronger frame returns; 351 Windsor replaces the 351M; blue oval replaces F-O-R-D on the hood.
302 gets multiport fuel injection (190 hp); Eddie Bauer package arrives. (A 210-hp 351 HO came for 1984.)
Fourth generation: new nose and dash, composite headlights, standard rear ABS, optional push-button 4WD, fuel-injected 300 six.
Fuel-injected 351; Mazda M5OD five-speed manual; transfer-case skid plate standard.
Overdrive automatics replace the C6: AOD (1990) and E4OD (1990 on).
Silver Anniversary Edition (Currant Red, gray leather) and Nite package; V8 and automatic only.
Fifth generation: rounder ninth-generation F-Series nose, revised dash, optional leather and power mirrors.
Driver's airbag; 300 six dropped; rear three-point belts and third brake light mount in the hardtop, which is now held on with security Torx bolts.
OBD-II engines; the first Ford with turn signals in the mirrors. The last Bronco is built on June 12, 1996.

identify.intro: Most full-size Broncos are what they claim to be. What you need to check is which generation and axle you are looking at, and whether a special edition is genuine.

items.head: Solid axle or TTB
items.body: Only 1978–79 trucks have the solid, coil-sprung Dana 44 front axle; everything from 1980 has the Twin Traction Beam, an independent design with a U-joint in the middle and the differential offset to the driver's side. A 1980–96 truck on a solid axle has been converted.

items.head: Faces by year
items.body: 1978 Customs had round headlights and Ranger XLTs rectangular ones, which became standard for 1979. 1980–81 trucks have F-O-R-D on the hood and 1982–86 trucks the blue oval. 1987–91 trucks have flush composite headlights, and 1992–96 trucks a rounder nose with a larger grille. Turn signals in the mirrors mean 1996.

items.head: Silver Anniversary Edition
items.body: 1991 only. Currant Red paint was exclusive to the package and came with a gray leather interior, the first leather in a Bronco. Like the Nite and Eddie Bauer, it came only with a V8 and an automatic.

items.head: Free Wheelin' and Nite
items.body: Free Wheelin' (1978–79, Custom or Ranger XLT) was a cosmetic package with tricolor stripes and blacked-out trim. Nite (1991–92) was blacked out with contrasting graphics.

items.head: Four doors
items.body: Ford never built a four-door 1978–96 Bronco. A four-door is a Centurion Classic C-150 or C-350, an F-Series crew cab joined to a Bronco rear body on a 140-in wheelbase.

capability.note: Three-across front bench and a folding, removable rear seat from 1978

values.intro: The 1978–79 solid-axle trucks are the collectible ones. The 1980–86 trucks sit in the middle, and the 1987–96 trucks remain the cheapest way into a Bronco, apart from special editions and low-mileage examples.
values.note: Based on Bring a Trailer sold results for the three model pages, mostly 2025–26: 24 recent results each for 1978–79, 1980–86 and 1987–96. The 1987–96 high outliers were a 1995 Eddie Bauer ($67,500) and an ex–'Stone Cold' Steve Austin 1995 XLT ($53,000).
